title: U.S. House · Kentucky's 6th District
area: Central Kentucky, including Lexington, Frankfort and Richmond.

context.text: This is an open seat. Incumbent Andy Barr (R) ran for U.S. Senate instead of re-election to this seat and did not appear on the District 6 primary ballot.

Ralph Alvarado defeated Ryan Dotson, Greg Plucinski, Steve Shannon and Adam Perez Arquette in the May 19, 2026 Republican primary. Zach Dembo defeated Cherlynn Stevenson, Erin Petrey and four other candidates in the Democratic primary.

summary.text: Zach Dembo is the Democratic nominee for Kentucky's 6th Congressional District. A Lexington native, he taught in the Mississippi Delta, served as a Navy JAG officer, worked as a federal prosecutor, and served in Gov. Andy Beshear's administration before resigning as an Assistant U.S. Attorney. He says he is running on a message of public service over politics.

background.text: Raised in Lexington; according to his campaign website, he is a ninth-generation Kentuckian whose family roots in Shelby and Henry counties trace back to the mid-1700s.
Attended Stanford University, then worked as an eighth-grade English teacher in the Mississippi Delta through Teach For America.
Earned a law degree from the University of Michigan Law School, where he commissioned as an officer in the U.S. Navy Judge Advocate General's (JAG) Corps, and served over four years on active duty.
In 2017 became a federal prosecutor in the U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division, prosecuting civil and constitutional rights cases.
In 2020 was appointed by Gov. Andy Beshear as a policy advisor and later legislative director.

Returned to federal prosecution as an Assistant United States Attorney in Lexington. According to his campaign website, he resigned after seeing what he describes as corruption and politicization of the Department of Justice.
Won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary for the seat with 39.6% of the vote in a multi-candidate field.
According to his campaign website, he lives in Lexington with his wife, Lindsey.

priorities.text: "My entire career has been devoted to public service, whether as a Navy JAG officer, a federal prosecutor protecting constitutional rights and fighting crime, or as a teacher in an underserved community. But after seeing the corruption in Washington D.C. and this Administration's abuse of the criminal justice system, I knew that my public service needed to take a different path."

summary.text: Ralph Alvarado is the Republican nominee for Kentucky's 6th Congressional District, a physician and former Kentucky state senator. He served in the state Senate from 2015 to 2023, was the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor in 2019, and left the Senate to become Tennessee's health commissioner. He campaigns primarily on healthcare, saying he wants to work across party lines to lower costs.

background.text: Born in San Jose, California.
Earned a bachelor of science degree and a medical degree from Loma Linda University and completed his medical residency at the University of Kentucky.
Worked as a physician with Kentucky One Medical Group; according to his campaign website, he has cared for patients across Central Kentucky for nearly three decades.

Served on the board of trustees of the Kentucky Medical Association, as a fellow and government council member of the American College of Physicians, and as a member of the Clark County Chamber of Commerce.
Elected to the Kentucky State Senate, District 28, in 2014, taking office January 1, 2015; his campaign website describes him as the first Hispanic member of the Kentucky General Assembly.
In the state Senate, he chaired the Health and Welfare Committee in the 2019-2020 and 2021-2022 sessions after serving as its vice chair earlier.
Was a delegate to the 2016 Republican National Convention and a member of the RNC Rules Committee.
Ran for lieutenant governor on a joint ticket with Gov. Matt Bevin in 2019; the ticket lost the general election, in which Democrat Jacqueline Coleman won the lieutenant governor race.
Resigned from the state Senate on January 6, 2023, to become commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Health.
According to his campaign website, he and his wife, Dawn, have been married for 32 years and raised two children in Clark County.

priorities.text: "Healthcare isn't a talking point to me — it's been my life's work. In Congress, I'll work with both parties to fight for affordable healthcare, lower costs, and practical solutions that help Kentucky families."

positions.summary: Campaigns primarily on lowering healthcare costs through bipartisan cooperation, without specifying support for a public-coverage expansion.
positions.quote: In Congress, I'll work with both parties to fight for affordable healthcare, lower costs, and practical solutions that help Kentucky families.

positions.summary: Voted yes on SB 9, which banned abortion once a fetal heartbeat is detectable, with exceptions.
Voted yes on SB 150, which eliminated Kentucky's permit requirement to carry a concealed deadly weapon.
Voted yes on HB 563, which created a tax-credit scholarship program funding private-school tuition and other education expenses for Kentucky students.

record.text: Chaired the Kentucky Senate Health and Welfare Committee during the 2019-2020 and 2021-2022 legislative sessions.
Voted yes on SB 9 (banning abortion once a fetal heartbeat is detectable, with limited exceptions), which passed the Kentucky Senate 31-6 on February 14, 2019.
Voted yes on SB 150 (eliminating the permit requirement to carry a concealed deadly weapon in Kentucky), which passed the Kentucky Senate 29-8 on February 14, 2019.
Voted yes on HB 563 (creating a tax-credit scholarship program funding private-school tuition and other education expenses), which passed the Kentucky Senate 21-15 on March 16, 2021.

summary.text: Pete Lynch is the Kentucky Party candidate for Kentucky's 6th Congressional District and a faculty member in the University of Kentucky Department of Political Science. In his Ballotpedia survey he says he has studied and taught political science for nearly a decade. He campaigns primarily on campaign finance reform, calling it the fundamental problem in American politics.

background.text: Is a faculty member of the Department of Political Science at the University of Kentucky, where, according to his Ballotpedia biography, he has studied and taught political science for nearly a decade.
Is on the 2026 general election ballot as the Kentucky Party candidate. He says he intends to get most of his donations from small donors.

priorities.text: "As someone who's studied and taught political science for nearly a decade, he understands that the fundamental problem in American politics is campaign funding."

Also supports a moratorium on AI data centers, restricting police access to license-plate-reader data such as Flock cameras without a warrant, moving toward Medicare for All, building affordable housing, cutting funding for Israel, and criminal justice reform to end mass incarceration.

positions.summary: Supports moving toward a Medicare for All system.
Supports cutting ties with, and funding for, Israel.

summary.text: Jay Bowman is an independent candidate for Kentucky's 6th Congressional District. Born in Michigan and raised in Utah, he says he started a business at 24 and has been a small-business owner in Kentucky since moving there in the mid-1990s. He campaigns on fiscal responsibility and a "10/10 Plan" to cut federal spending and reduce the deficit.

background.text: Says he was born in Michigan and raised in Utah, where his father's small-business success inspired him and his mother's pursuit of education instilled a love of learning.
Says he started his own business at 24, moved to Kentucky in the mid-1990s, and has raised his family there as a small business owner.
Is on the 2026 general election ballot as an independent.

priorities.text: Says he will work for young Kentuckians, focusing on fiscal responsibility and reducing what he calls wasteful spending.

summary.text: Robert Quigley is an independent write-in candidate for Kentucky's 6th Congressional District. No campaign website, public statements, or biographical profile were found for this candidate.

researchNotes: Open seat: Andy Barr, the sitting representative, ran for U.S. Senate instead. No detailed issue positions beyond general priorities were found for Dembo or Bowman. No public information beyond his name on the ballot was found for write-in candidate Robert Quigley. Biographical information for Lynch and Bowman comes from their own Ballotpedia survey responses; no independent coverage was found, and none beyond his name on the ballot for Quigley.
